title: “HE WENT IN TO HER”: Why Does the Bible Use This Phrase for Sex?
paragraphs: “HE WENT IN TO HER”: Why Does the Bible Use This Phrase for Sex?

The strange biblical expression modern readers sometimes laugh at was never meant to be crude—and once you understand what the ancient words are actually doing, you may never read these passages the same way again.
“He went in to her.”
There it is.
A phrase sitting quietly in the pages of Scripture that can make a modern reader stop, reread the sentence, and wonder:
Wait… does that mean what I think it means?
Sometimes it does.
But perhaps not in quite the way you have been taught to hear it.
Because when an ancient Hebrew writer says that a man “went in to” a woman, you are not necessarily looking at an awkward ancient attempt to avoid saying “they had sex.”
You are looking through the window of another language.
Another culture.
Another world.

And if we force twenty-first-century English assumptions into that ancient window, we can easily turn something serious into something ridiculous—or make the Bible say more than the Hebrew itself actually says.
That matters.

Especially because some of the passages containing this expression are surrounded by marriage, desire, betrayal, infertility, power, family conflict, prostitution, adultery, exploitation, judgment, covenant, childbirth, and consequences that echo through generations.
The Bible does not sanitize humanity.
It tells us what people actually did.
Sometimes faithfully.
Sometimes foolishly.
Sometimes beautifully.
Sometimes horribly.
And then, astonishingly, it shows us what God can do with people whose stories have become painfully complicated.
That is where this becomes much bigger than an unusual phrase about sex.
Because perhaps you came here curious about three ancient words.
But before we are finished, they may lead us somewhere much closer to home.
They may lead us into the rooms we keep locked.
The memories we don't discuss.
The choices we wish could be unwritten.
And eventually…
to Jesus.
The Hebrew expression behind many translations of “went in to her” involves the extremely common verb בּוֹא (boʾ), meaning fundamentally “to come” or “to enter.”
In Genesis 16:2, for example, Sarai tells Abram concerning Hagar:
בֹּא־נָא אֶל־שִׁפְחָתִי
bo-na el-shifchati
In very wooden English, something like:
“Please, go/come in to my female servant.”
The following verse explains that Sarai gives Hagar to Abram as a wife, and Genesis 16:4 continues:
וַיָּבֹא אֶל־הָגָר
vayyavo el-Hagar
“And he went in to Hagar…”
Then Scripture immediately tells us:
וַתַּהַר
vattahar
“And she conceived.”
There is no serious mystery about what occurred in that narrative.
Abram had sexual relations with Hagar.
But notice something important.
The Hebrew verb בוא itself does not inherently mean “to have sex.”
That distinction protects us from a surprisingly common mistake.
בוא is an ordinary Hebrew verb for coming, arriving, or entering. Context and construction determine when the expression carries a sexual sense.
In other words, you cannot simply open the Hebrew Bible, find בוא, and translate every occurrence sexually.
That would produce absurd results.
Language does not work that way.
English does something similar.
If someone says, “They slept together,” the individual words slept and together do not inherently mean sexual intercourse. Context produces the idiomatic meaning.
Likewise, biblical Hebrew can use ordinary vocabulary in contexts where the intended meaning becomes unmistakably sexual.
And Scripture has other vocabulary for sexual relations as well.
One of the most famous examples appears only a few chapters earlier:
“Now Adam knew Eve his wife…”
The Hebrew is:
וְהָאָדָם יָדַע אֶת־חַוָּה אִשְׁתּוֹ
veha-adam yada et-Chavvah ishto
The key verb is יָדַע (yadaʿ)—“to know.”
Again, the ordinary Hebrew verb does not automatically mean sex.
A person can “know” information.
Know another person.
Know something by experience.
But Genesis 4:1 supplies the context:
Adam “knew” Eve…
and she conceived Cain.
The sexual meaning is therefore clear.
This should immediately tell us something about reading Scripture responsibly.
Biblical language about sex is neither merely clinical nor uniformly euphemistic.
The biblical writers use several expressions depending upon context.
Sometimes the language emphasizes knowing.
Sometimes lying with someone.
Sometimes coming or going in to someone.
Sometimes the language becomes disturbingly direct because the event being described is disturbing.
And sometimes modern English translations understandably render an ancient idiom by its meaning rather than reproducing its structure word-for-word.
That is translation.
A “literal” translation is not always the translation that copies every ancient word with the nearest English word.
A faithful translation must ask:
What did this expression communicate to its original audience?
That question becomes especially important with the Hebrew expression commonly translated “went in to her.”
It is tempting to preach an entire theology from the English word “in.”
We should resist that temptation.
The phrase is not a secret anatomical code inserted into Scripture so that modern readers can discover a hidden doctrine of sexuality.
Nor should every occurrence be romanticized.
Sometimes the surrounding relationship is profoundly broken.
Genesis 16 is the perfect warning.
Abram going in to Hagar resulted in conception.
But the narrative surrounding that conception is hardly a sentimental portrait of marital intimacy.
Sarai was unable to bear children.
She gave Hagar, her Egyptian servant, to Abram.
Hagar conceived.
Conflict erupted.
Sarai dealt harshly with her.
Hagar fled.
Human beings tried to manage God's promise through their own arrangements, and a vulnerable woman became entangled in the consequences.
Yet this is where Scripture does something extraordinary.
God sees Hagar.
The woman caught inside someone else's plan becomes the woman who encounters the God who sees her.
She says:
אַתָּה אֵל רֳאִי
Attah El Ro'i
“You are a God of seeing,” commonly expressed as “the God who sees me.”
Think about that.
The story begins with people deciding what will be done with Hagar's body.
But God does not treat Hagar as scenery.
He sees her.
He speaks to her.
He knows her suffering.
That does not mean every human action in the chapter receives divine approval.
This is one of the most important principles for reading biblical narratives:
Description is not automatically prescription.
If Scripture tells you that someone did something, that does not automatically mean God commands, endorses, or celebrates it.
The Bible records lies without commanding lying.
It records murder without endorsing murder.
It records adultery without blessing adultery.
It records polygamous households without pretending those households were free of devastating conflict.
It records sexual sin without turning sexual sin into righteousness.
The Bible is brutally honest about humanity because redemption only makes sense when we understand what humanity needs redemption from.
And this is where the phrase “he went in to her” becomes more than a linguistic curiosity.
Follow that expression through biblical narratives and you repeatedly encounter consequences.
Bodies matter.
Sex matters.
Promises matter.
Marriage matters.
Faithfulness matters.
People matter.
Sex in Scripture is never reduced to the modern slogan that whatever happens between consenting adults is automatically spiritually insignificant.
At the same time, the Bible's sexual ethic must never become an excuse for treating sexually broken people as permanently contaminated.
Because the Gospel does not tell sinners:
“Clean yourself until Jesus can tolerate you.”
The Gospel announces that Christ came for sinners.
There is a difference between grace and permission.
Grace does not rename darkness as light.
Grace walks into darkness carrying light.
Jesus could say to the woman caught in adultery, “Neither do I condemn you,” and also call her away from sin.
Mercy and holiness were never enemies in Him.
We often separate them.
Jesus did not.
That matters because someone reading this has sexual history attached to their name.
Maybe nobody knows.
Maybe everybody knows.
Maybe your first sexual experience was something precious within marriage.
Maybe it wasn't.
Maybe you crossed boundaries knowingly.
Maybe boundaries were crossed against you.
Those realities must never be confused.
What was done to you is not automatically a sin committed by you.
Perhaps you cheated.
Perhaps someone cheated on you.
Perhaps pornography became the room you entered whenever loneliness became unbearable.
Perhaps you learned to use another person's body as medicine for your own emptiness.
Perhaps someone used yours.

Perhaps you have carried an abortion, an affair, a secret relationship, sexual exploitation, prostitution, promiscuity, lust, shame, or memories you would erase instantly if life came with a delete button.
Maybe you have been in church for years while hiding a second life.
You sing.
You smile.
You say, “God is good.”
People call you faithful.
And somewhere behind the smile is a locked door.
You know exactly what is behind it.
So does God.
And this is where many people misunderstand Christianity.
They think Christianity says:
God discovered your scandal.
Now run.
The Gospel says something far more terrifying and far more beautiful:
God already knew.
And Christ came anyway.
“For all have sinned and fall short of the glory of God.”
Romans does not say some.
It says all.
But Paul does not stop there.
Those who are justified are justified by God's grace through the redemption that is in Christ Jesus.
That word “redemption” matters.
In Greek, Paul uses ἀπολύτρωσις (apolytrōsis), language associated with release or liberation through redemption.
Christianity is not ultimately the story of morally impressive people showing God why they deserve heaven.
It is the story of sinners who could never purchase their own rescue being redeemed through Christ.
And redemption cost something.
Not silver.
Not religious performance.
Not your ability to pretend.
Peter writes:
The cross destroys two lies simultaneously.
The first lie says:
“My sin isn't really that serious.”
Look at Calvary.
Sin is serious.
The second lie says:
“My sin is too serious for God to forgive.”
Look again at Calvary.
Grace is greater.
Jesus was not crucified because humanity needed motivational advice.
He was crucified because reconciliation with a holy God required something sinners could never accomplish for themselves.
And He rose.
That matters just as much as the blood.
Christian faith does not end at a grave containing a heroic martyr.
The apostolic proclamation is that Jesus Christ was crucified, buried, and raised.
Death did not get the final sentence.
Sin did not get the final sentence.
Shame did not get the final sentence.
Your worst chapter does not have authority to write the ending if your life has been surrendered to Jesus Christ.
This is why the biblical story is filled with people whose histories would make religious people uncomfortable.
Judah.
Read Genesis 38 slowly.
Judah sees a woman he believes to be a prostitute.
He propositions her.
He gives her identifying possessions as a pledge.
Later, when Tamar is reported pregnant, Judah is prepared to condemn her.
Then the evidence arrives.
His seal.
His cord.
His staff.
His secret suddenly has his name written all over it.
And Judah says:
צָדְקָה מִמֶּנִּי
tzadqah mimmeni
“She is more righteous than I.”
The man prepared to expose another person is exposed himself.
Have you ever noticed how easily we become furious at sins in other people while carefully managing the lighting around our own?
We know how to crop our lives.
We know what to post.
We know what testimony version sounds respectable.
We know which details to leave outside the frame.
But Scripture refuses to crop the family album.
And centuries later, Matthew opens his Gospel with the genealogy of Jesus Christ.
Judah is there.
Tamar is there.
David is there.
The wife of Uriah is deliberately recalled.
Human sin is not erased from the historical road leading to Bethlehem.
Yet neither does sin conquer God's redemptive purpose.
Be careful here.
This does not mean sin was necessary so grace could happen.
It does not mean evil becomes good because God can redeem people from evil.
Paul explicitly rejects the idea that Christians should continue in sin so grace may increase.
Grace is not God's permission slip for rebellion.
Grace is God's rescue of rebels.
And that rescue has a name.
Jesus.
Ἰησοῦς.
Iēsous.
The New Testament's Greek form of the name corresponding to Hebrew/Aramaic Yeshua.
Matthew tells us why the child receives this name:
“He will save his people from their sins.”
Not merely from embarrassment.
Not merely from consequences.
Not merely from low self-esteem.
From their sins.
There is the heartbeat of Christianity.
Jesus does not merely improve your scandal.
He saves sinners.
He forgives.
He cleanses.
He reconciles.
He calls us to repent.
The New Testament word μετάνοια (metanoia) refers to repentance—a genuine turning of heart and life toward God.
Repentance is not theatrical self-hatred.
It is not endlessly punishing yourself so God will finally believe you are sorry.
Repentance agrees with God about sin and turns toward Him.
It stops defending what Christ died to save us from.
It stops calling chains jewelry.
It stops calling captivity freedom.
It stops saying, “This is just who I am,” when Jesus is calling us to become new.
Maybe that is why you are still reading.
Perhaps you thought you clicked an article about a strange biblical phrase.
But something else has been reading you.
“He went in to her.”
An ancient expression.
A human act.
A consequence.
A story.
And behind thousands of years of biblical stories stands the same uncomfortable truth:
Human beings keep entering places we were warned not to enter.
Not only bedrooms.
Secret conversations.
Hidden browser tabs.
Relationships.
Bitterness.
Pride.
Greed.
Envy.
Self-righteousness.
The private fantasy.
The emotional affair.
The message we delete afterward.
The compromise nobody sees.
The addiction we renamed “stress relief.”
The grudge we renamed “discernment.”
The gossip we renamed “concern.”
The arrogance we renamed “conviction.”
We enter.
Then we discover that some doors are much easier to enter than to leave.
And still…
Jesus comes looking for sinners.
Not to participate in our darkness.
To bring us out of it.
That is why the Gospel is scandalous in the best sense.
The holy Son of God receives repentant sinners.
People with histories.
People with screenshots.
People with secrets.
People with reputations.
People who wasted years.
People who knew better.
People who didn't.
People who cannot undo yesterday.
Jesus does not require you to travel backward through time.
He calls you to come to Him now.
Confess.
Repent.
Believe.
Follow.
John writes:
Notice what the verse does not say.
“If we conceal our sins convincingly…”
“If we punish ourselves sufficiently…”
“If we become respectable enough…”
“If we wait until our history stops hurting…”
No.
Confession.
Forgiveness.
Cleansing.
The Greek verb commonly translated “confess” there is ὁμολογέω (homologeō), carrying the idea of acknowledging or confessing.
Stop hiding.
Not because everyone on Facebook needs every detail of your private history.
They don't.
Wisdom still matters.
Privacy still matters.
Other people's dignity still matters.
But you cannot heal spiritually while building your identity around deception before God.
He already knows.
The question is not whether He can see behind the door.
The question is whether you will finally stop pretending the door is not there.
Somebody needs to whisper this before reading another sentence:
“Jesus, I need Your mercy.”
Not because the sentence itself saves you.
Jesus saves.
But because perhaps tonight is the night pretending finally becomes exhausting.
Maybe you have spent years believing that your sexual past disqualified you from being loved by God.
Hear the Gospel carefully.
Your past cannot be made righteous by pretending it was righteous.
But neither is your past stronger than Christ's ability to redeem.
Paul reminded the Corinthian church of patterns of sin that characterized their former lives, including sexual immorality.
Then comes one of Scripture's most beautiful reversals:
“And such were some of you.”
Were.
“But you were washed…”
“But you were sanctified…”
“But you were justified in the name of the Lord Jesus Christ and by the Spirit of our God.”
That is not cheap grace.
That is transformation.
Christianity does not say:
“I found Jesus, therefore nothing about my life needs to change.”
It says:
Jesus found me in death and called me into life.
So if you are sleeping with someone who is not your spouse and conviction is pressing against your heart, do not silence it.
If pornography owns part of your life, bring it into the light and seek wise, trustworthy help.
If you are married and emotionally drifting toward someone else, stop romanticizing the edge of the cliff.
If you betrayed your spouse, repentance requires more than feeling guilty when you get caught.
If you have been sinned against sexually, please hear this with absolute clarity:
Another person's evil does not make you spiritually filthy.
Abuse is not consensual sexual sin.
The shame belongs to the wrongdoing, not to the wounded person merely because they were wounded.
Jesus is not standing over survivors asking why they were harmed.
He is near to the brokenhearted.
And if you are the person who caused harm, do not use Christian forgiveness language to escape accountability.
Repentance does not manipulate victims into silence.
Grace is not obstruction.
Forgiveness does not magically erase every earthly consequence.
The Gospel gives no predator permission to weaponize “grace” against the people they hurt.
Real repentance comes into the light.
This is what makes biblical grace so much stronger than sentimental grace.
Sentimental grace says:
“It doesn't matter.”
Biblical grace says:
It mattered enough for Christ to die…
and Christ loves sinners enough not to leave repentant people enslaved to it.
Maybe this exposed something hidden.
If it did, you don't have to publish your private details. But you can make a simple declaration of surrender.
There are moments when three words can be the beginning of stepping out of isolation.
Someone reading the comments may realize they are not the only believer still fighting.
Someone may pray for you.
Someone may finally admit they need help too.
That is what Christian community should be.
Not a museum of people pretending they never broke.
A family gathered around the One who saves.
And perhaps someone you love needs this article.
Not because you want to embarrass them.
Don't weaponize it.
But if a friend has been drowning quietly in shame, send it privately.
Sometimes evangelism begins with something as ordinary as pressing Share.
And invite your family, your friends, struggling believers, seekers, lukewarm Christians—and even the person who does not yet believe—to follow too.
Not to build a religious fan club.
To keep putting the Gospel in places where people are already scrolling.
If those resources and articles have helped you, there is another way you can participate.
But hear this carefully because money and ministry must never be manipulated.
It does not buy forgiveness.
It does not increase the power of your prayers.
It does not replace faith, repentance, obedience, generosity to those in need, or faithful participation in a local church.
The New Testament repeatedly emphasizes willing, cheerful, non-coerced generosity.
Paul writes in 2 Corinthians 9:7 that giving should not be “reluctantly or under compulsion,” because God loves a cheerful giver.
That means Christian support should never sound like:
“Pay us or you are failing God.”
It should sound like:
“If this work is bearing Gospel fruit and you freely want to help sustain and expand it, you are invited to participate.”
That is the invitation.
Not because God needs your money.
But because ministry in this world requires people willing to give, serve, share, pray, create, distribute, and support.
If you have been asking, “How can I help Gospel Warrior reach more people?” this is one concrete way.
But the merchandise is not the mission.
Jesus is.
The discount is simply gratitude.
The goal is discipleship.
The goal is truth.
The goal is putting Scripture in front of one more exhausted believer at midnight.
One more marriage hanging by a thread.
One more person hiding an addiction.
One more skeptic willing to read.
One more ashamed Christian wondering whether Jesus still receives repentant sinners.
One more soul discovering that the cross is not religious decoration.
It is an announcement:
There is mercy.
There is forgiveness.
There is redemption.
There is a way home.
Pray.
Send it privately to somebody who needs it.
Tag people when doing so would encourage rather than embarrass them.
Invite others to follow.
Because you never know which share will land on a screen at exactly the moment somebody has decided they are too dirty for God.
You never know which person is sitting alone thinking:
“If everyone knew, nobody would love me.”
Maybe they need to discover what Scripture actually says.
Maybe they need to meet the Jesus who ate with sinners without becoming like them.
The Jesus who spoke truth without surrendering compassion.
The Jesus who called people to repentance without treating broken people as disposable.
The Jesus who carried a cross.
The Jesus who died.
The Jesus who rose.
The Jesus who still saves.
And now perhaps that strange phrase that brought you here feels different.
“He went in to her.”
At first it sounded almost amusing.
Ancient.
Awkward.
Something to investigate linguistically.
But Scripture would not let us stay on the surface.
Because beneath the phrase were people.
Beneath the people were choices.
Beneath the choices were wounds, desires, sins, consequences, pregnancies, families, conflicts, and stories.
And beneath the brokenness was a God who refused to abandon His redemptive purpose.
The God who saw Hagar.
The God who exposed Judah.
The God who remembered Tamar.
The God who worked through generations of deeply imperfect human beings.
The God who sent His Son.
Jesus did not enter history through a spotless human family tree filled with people who had never needed grace.
He entered our actual world.
A world of scandal.
A world of lust.
A world of violence.
A world of betrayal.
A world of religious hypocrisy.
A world of wounded women and sinful men.
A world frighteningly similar to ours.
And into that world came the Word made flesh.
Not to tell darkness that darkness was actually light.
Not to tell sinners that sin didn't matter.
But to save.
Perhaps your story contains a chapter you wish God had never seen.
He saw it.
And the cross still happened.
Perhaps your story contains something you have never told another human being.
God knows it.
And Jesus still says, “Come.”
Come honestly.
Come repentantly.
Come without the costume.
Come without editing the testimony first.
Come because sinners do not wash themselves before coming to the fountain.
They come because they need washing.
Maybe your scandal happened ten years ago.
Maybe last night.
Maybe you are still inside it.
Then don't turn this article into another emotional moment you forget tomorrow.
Turn toward Christ.
Seek wise pastoral help.
Make whatever confession and restitution genuine repentance requires without unnecessarily exposing or harming innocent people.
Break the secret arrangement.
Close the hidden account.
End the affair.
Ask for help with the addiction.
Tell the truth.
Return to Scripture.
Return to prayer.
Return to Christian community.
And where serious harm or abuse has occurred, seek appropriate professional, pastoral, and legal help rather than trying to bury it beneath religious language.
Grace is not hiding.
Grace is being found.
And if this article reached somewhere deeper than you expected, be honest about that too.
You don't have to tell strangers every detail.
Just don't keep telling Jesus there is nothing behind the door.
Because the greatest truth in this entire article was never hidden inside the Hebrew phrase.
It was waiting at the cross.
Your sin can tell the truth about where you have been.
Your scars can tell the truth about what you survived.
Your consequences can tell the truth about what happened.
But none of them gets to sit on the throne.
Jesus does.
And for the person who turns to Him, the final word is not scandal.
It is grace.
The chapter you are most ashamed to let anyone read may become the very page where people discover just how much rewriting grace can do.
